141: Hill introduces 'TAKE INVENTORY OF YOURSELF: 28 Questions You Should Answer.' Annual self-analysis is as essential as annual inventory in merchandising—the yearly analysis should disclose decreased faults and increased virtues. One goes ahead, stands still, or goes backward; the object should be to go ahead. Analysis should be made at year's end to include improvements in New Year's Resolutions. He presents the Self-Analysis Questionnaire: (1) Have I attained my yearly goal? (2) Have I delivered service of the best possible QUALITY? (3) Have I delivered service in the greatest possible QUANTITY? (4) Has my conduct been harmonious and cooperative? (5) Has PROCRASTINATION decreased my efficiency, and to what extent? (6) Have I improved my PERSONALITY, and how? (7) Have I been PERSISTENT in following plans through? (8) Have I reached DECISIONS PROMPTLY AND DEFINITELY? (9) Have any of the Six Basic Fears decreased my efficiency? (10) Have I been over-cautious or under-cautious?
142: The self-analysis questions continue: (11) Has my relationship with associates been pleasant or unpleasant, and if unpleasant, was the fault mine? (12) Have I dissipated energy through lack of CONCENTRATION? (13) Have I been open-minded and tolerant? (14) In what way have I improved my ability to render service? (15) Have I been intemperate in any habits? (16) Have I expressed EGOTISM openly or secretly? (17) Has my conduct induced associates to RESPECT me? (18) Have my opinions and DECISIONS been based on guesswork or accurate analysis and THOUGHT? (19) Have I budgeted time, expenses, and income conservatively? (20) How much time have I devoted to UNPROFITABLE effort? (21) How may I REBUDGET my time and change habits for greater efficiency? (22) Have I been guilty of conduct not approved by my conscience? (23) In what ways have I rendered MORE SERVICE than I was paid to render? (24) Have I been unfair to anyone? (25) If I had been the purchaser of my own services, would I be satisfied? (26) Am I in the right vocation? (27) Has the purchaser of my services been satisfied? (28) What is my present rating on the fundamental principles of success?—rate fairly and have it checked by someone courageous enough to do it accurately.
143: Hill states that having read and assimilated this chapter, readers are ready to create a practical plan for marketing personal services. The chapter contains every essential principle: leadership attributes, causes of leadership failure, fields of opportunity, causes of failure in all walks of life, and self-analysis questions. This detailed information is included because it's needed by all who must begin accumulating riches by marketing personal services—those who lost jobs, property, fortunes, and beginners have nothing but personal services to offer. The information is valuable for aspiring leaders in any calling, particularly business or industrial executives. It also helps one become more analytical and capable of judging people—priceless for personnel directors and supervisors. Hill challenges readers to test the soundness by answering the 28 questions in writing. He then introduces 'Where and How One May Find Opportunities to Accumulate Riches,' asking where one can apply these principles. He begins by taking inventory of what America offers: freedom of thought and deed unequaled anywhere—freedom of expression, education, religion, politics, business choice, property accumulation, residence, marriage, equal opportunity, travel, food choice, and freedom to AIM FOR ANY STATION IN LIFE.
144: Hill notes these freedoms constitute OPPORTUNITY of the highest order, conspicuous because America is the only country guaranteeing such broad freedoms to every citizen. He then recounts blessings available to the average American family. (a) FOOD: the average family has the choicest food selection at affordable prices. He provides a detailed cost breakdown of a simple breakfast for a family of four in a small to medium-size American city: orange juice from Florida ($.56), cereal from Kansas ($.44), tea from China ($.20), bananas from South America ($.28), toasted bread from Kansas ($.19), fresh eggs from a regional farm ($.18), sugar from Utah/Texas ($.01), margarine from Illinois ($.16), milk from a local dairy ($.74)—grand total $2.76, approximately 69 cents per person. This breakfast was gathered from China, South America, Utah, Kansas, and Illinois and delivered ready for consumption in the heart of an American city, at a cost within the means of the most humble laborer, including all taxes.
145: Hill continues inventorying American blessings. (b) SHELTER: the family lives in a comfortable apartment with natural gas heating, electricity, and gas cooking for $800/month (or $685 in smaller cities). The apartment contains an electric toaster ($15), vacuum cleaner, hot and cold water, refrigerator, and various electrical conveniences. The wife curls hair, washes and dries clothes with electrical equipment. The husband shaves with an electric razor. They receive worldwide entertainment 24 hours daily without charge via television or radio. (c) CLOTHING: the average woman can dress comfortably for less than $1,500/year, and the average man for the same or less. Beyond basic necessities, average Americans enjoy automobile transportation, security of property rights (government-protected bank deposits), passport-free interstate travel by car, plane, bus, train, or ship. Hill then introduces 'The Miracle That Has Provided These Blessings,' promising to analyze the source of America's freedoms and opportunities.
146: Hill identifies the mysterious benefactor as CAPITAL—not just money, but highly organized, intelligent groups who plan ways to use money efficiently for public good and personal profit. These groups include scientists, educators, chemists, inventors, business analysts, advertising executives, transportation experts, accountants, lawyers, doctors, and specialists in all fields. They pioneer, experiment, build roads, support colleges and hospitals, publish newspapers, operate broadcast stations, pay most government costs, and handle details essential to human progress. Capitalists are the brains of civilization. Money without brains is dangerous; properly used, it's civilization's most important essential. The simple breakfast couldn't be delivered at 69 cents per person without organized capital providing machinery, ships, railroads, trucks, and trained workers. Hill challenges readers to imagine collecting and delivering that breakfast without capital: swimming to China for tea, walking to Utah or Texas for sugar, to Florida for orange juice, to Kansas for wheat bread. Cereal would have to be omitted—it requires trained organization and machinery, all calling for CAPITAL.
147: Hill continues the thought experiment: you'd swim to South America for bananas, walk to the nearest dairy for milk, do without margarine (requires capital for manufacture). Then your family could enjoy breakfast, and you'd collect your six dimes and seven pennies for your labor! This absurd scenario illustrates the only way food could reach the breakfast table without a capitalistic system. The billions required for railroads, ships, and trucking lines stagger imagination, plus armies of trained employees. Transportation is only part—before hauling, something must be grown or manufactured, requiring more billions for equipment, machinery, boxing, marketing, and wages. Ships, railroads, and trucking don't spring from earth automatically—they come through labor, ingenuity, and organizing ability of people with IMAGINATION, FAITH, ENTHUSIASM, DECISION, and PERSISTENCE. These capitalists are motivated by desire to build, achieve, render useful service, earn profits, and accumulate riches. Because they RENDER SERVICE WITHOUT WHICH THERE WOULD BE NO CIVILIZATION, they put themselves in the way of great riches. Hill acknowledges these are the same people radicals and politicians call 'predatory interests' or 'Wall Street' or 'big business.'
148: Hill clarifies he's not arguing for or against any group or economic system, not condemning collective bargaining or giving all capitalists a clean bill of health. His purpose—faithfully pursued for over 25 years—is to present the most dependable philosophy for accumulating riches. He analyzed the capitalistic system's advantages to show: (1) all who seek riches must recognize and adapt to the system controlling approaches to fortunes, and (2) to present the side opposite politicians and demagogues who deliberately becloud issues by treating organized capital as poisonous. America was developed through capital; those seeking riches must understand that neither riches nor opportunity would exist without ORGANIZED CAPITAL. Hill criticizes the popular pastime of radicals, self-seeking politicians, racketeers, and crooked labor leaders taking potshots at 'Wall Street' and 'Big Business.' During the Depression, high government officials lined up with cheap politicians and labor leaders to throttle the system making America the richest country on earth. This alliance prolonged the worst depression America had ever known, costing millions their jobs.
149: Hill describes how certain labor leaders joined politicians, offering to deliver voters in return for legislation permitting people to TAKE RICHES AWAY FROM INDUSTRY BY ORGANIZED FORCE instead of giving fair work for fair pay. Millions still try to GET WITHOUT GIVING—demanding shorter hours and more pay, or demanding government relief without working. Hill acknowledges this is a free country where everyone may think as they please and many live with little effort. However, he warns that FREEDOM cannot bring riches without effort. The only dependable method of accumulating and legally holding riches is rendering useful service. No system allows legally acquiring riches through force of numbers without giving equivalent value. He introduces the LAW OF ECONOMICS—a law no one can beat, more powerful than all politicians and political machines, beyond control of special interest groups and labor unions. It cannot be bribed. IT HAS AN ALL-SEEING EYE AND A PERFECT SYSTEM OF BOOKKEEPING, keeping accurate accounts of everyone trying to get without giving. Sooner or later its auditors demand an accounting.
150: Hill states that 'Wall Street' and 'Big Business' represent people who understand, respect, and adapt to the LAW OF ECONOMICS—their financial continuation depends on it. Most Americans like this country and its capitalistic system; those who don't have the privilege of leaving. America provides all the freedom and opportunity any honest person needs. When hunting game, one selects grounds where game is plentiful—the same applies to seeking riches. He lists staggering annual consumer spending figures: $29 billion for hair/nail/skin care, $25 billion for newspapers, $31 billion on books, $14 billion on sound recordings, $54 billion on motion pictures, $115 billion on fast food, $13.3 billion on bar/tavern tabs, $34 billion on toys, $38 billion on lawn/garden care, $74 billion on sporting goods, $91 billion on furniture, $167 billion on clothing, $22 billion on laundry/dry cleaning, $87 billion in appliance/electronics stores, and $14 billion for burial. These represent vast OPPORTUNITY. Producing, transporting, and marketing these items gives regular employment to millions who receive billions monthly. There is nothing to stop anyone from engaging in any portion of this effort. CAPITALISTIC AMERICA ENSURES EVERY PERSON THE OPPORTUNITY TO RENDER USEFUL SERVICE AND COLLECT RICHES IN PROPORTION TO THE VALUE OF SERVICE RENDERED. The system cannot promise SOMETHING FOR NOTHING because it's controlled by the LAW OF ECONOMICS.
